171. Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent.--

26. As a cardinal rule of criminal jurisprudence, the prosecution has to stand on its own legs and cannot point out the lacunae in the defence case to earn a conviction.

27. PW-1, during his cross-examination has stated that he was called to the Police Station and was asked to identify the accused person through a glass-window and the accused was correctly identified by the complainant.
It is a matter of record that the accused had refused to participate in the TIP Proceedings stating that his photographs were taken by the Police and the same might have been shown to the witness.

28. The law as regards the TIP Proceedings is settled and was reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Mukesh v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2017) 6 SCC 1 that the identification parades belong to the stage of investigation, and there is no provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure which obliges the investigating agency to hold, or confers a right upon the accused to claim a test identification parade.

Failure to hold a test identification parade would not make inadmissible the evidence of identification in court.
The weight to be attached to such identification should be a matter for the courts of fact.

It is well settled that the substantive evidence is the evidence of identification in court and the test identification parade provides corroboration to the identification of the witness in court, if required.
However, what weight must be attached to the evidence of identification in court, which is not preceded by a test identification parade, is a matter for the courts of fact to examine.
Even if there is no previous TIP, the court may appreciate the dock identification as being above board and more than conclusive.

39. The complainant, during his examination as PW-1, reiterated the above incident and thus has corroborated the story of the prosecution.
He had also identified the accused.
During his cross-examination, PW-1 has deposed that he was given four slaps by the accused, however, no visible injury was found.
Thus, even during the cross-examination, nothing has come on record to cast any doubt on the testimony of the complainant.
Accordingly, the testimony of PW-1 has remained uncontroverted.
40. In the present matter, the complainant is the injured victim.
The law as regards appreciation of testimony of the injured witness is settled that his presence at the spot of occurrence cannot be doubted.
Such a witness' statement is generally considered to be very reliable and it is unlikely that he would let the actual assailant go scot-free in order to falsely implicate someone else.

The testimony of an injured witness has its own relevancy and efficacy, as he has sustained injuries at the time and place of occurrence and this lends support to his testimony that he was present during the occurrence.
Thus, the testimony of an injured witness is accorded a special status in law.

28. The law as regards the TIP Proceedings is settled and was reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Mukesh v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2017) 6 SCC 1 that the identification parades belong to the stage of investigation, and there is no provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure which obliges the investigating agency to hold, or confers a right upon the accused to claim a test identification parade.

Failure to hold a test identification parade would not make inadmissible the evidence of identification in court.
The weight to be attached to such identification should be a matter for the courts of fact.
It is well settled that the substantive evidence is the evidence of identification in court and the test identification parade provides corroboration to the identification of the witness in court, if required.
However, what weight must be attached to the evidence of identification in court, which is not preceded by a test identification parade, is a matter for the courts of fact to examine.
Even if there is no previous TIP, the court may appreciate the dock identification as being above board and more than conclusive.
In Ousu Varghese v. State of Kerala (1974) 3 SCC 767, it has been held that held that minor variations in the accounts of the witnesses are often the hallmark of the truth of their testimony.

minor discrepancies on trivial matters, which do not affect the core of the prosecution's case, may not prompt the court to reject the evidence in its entirety.
